To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
cross-presentation of human viruses by DC is a very efficient mechanism for the activation of virus-specific CTL and that the DC subset most suitable for this task is the monocyte-derived DC.
cross-presentation by DC is an efficient mechanism for initiation of CTL immunity against viruses that infect DC as well as viruses that do not directly infect DC.

human DC are able to cross-present viral antigens from a broad variety of viruses, including HIV, HCV, and influenza, and that cross-presentation of these viral antigens by human DC is an efficient way to initiate virus-specific CTL immunity, which is important for effective viral clearance.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the understanding of how human DC initiate virus-specific CD8(+) cytotoxic T lymphocyte (CTL) responses.
the understanding of how DC induce anti-viral immunity.
the understanding of the mechanism of viral MHC class I antigen presentation by human DC and the identification of the preferred DC subsets for effective anti-viral CTL responses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
human DC are capable of MHC class I antigen presentation of viral antigenunder a variety of conditions, which is a prerequisite for effective induction of CTL responses.

the most important DC subsets for the induction of effective CTL responses against viral infections are the plasmacytoid DC (pDC) and the myeloid DC subsets, which include the classical monocyte-derived DC, the monocyte-derived DC precursors (moDCp), and the monocyte-derived Langerhans cells (Langerhans cell precursors (LangerhCP)).
cross-presentation of virus antigens by human DC is the preferred mechanism to initiate virus-specific CTL, but that this is not necessarily always the case.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
cross-presentation of virus-specific CD4+ T helper cells is not only important for the initiation of CTL responses but also for the maintenance of CTL responses.

cross-priming of CTL is an important mechanism for the initiation of virus-specific CTL responses and that the cross-presentation capacity of DC can be enhanced by targeting DC with viral antigens or by manipulating DC in such a way that the cross-presenter capacity of DC is enhanced.
the cross-presentation pathway can be exploited to induce virus-specific CD8 T cell responses, which can be achieved by targeting the appropriate DC subset and by providing sufficient antigen.
The main takeaway from our work is that

cross-presentation by human DC is not only a very effective way to induce virus-specific CD8 T cell immunity, but that it is also a very efficient and rapid way to induce virus specific CD8 T cell responses.

cross-presentation of antigens by human DC is a very effective mechanism to initiate immunity to viral infections and that the most efficient DC subsets for cross-presentation are CD1c+ and CD141+ DC, which are the main DC subsets that are present in human lymphoid tissue and that can be easily isolated in sufficient quantities.

cross-presentation by DC can be a powerful strategy to activate CTL responses against viruses and that the rational use of the different DC subsets is important to optimize the induction of virus specific CTL.
